turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hello, Doctor. Well, I came in because... I just can’t seem to get anything in order anymore. It's really getting out of hand. If you saw my kitchen table right now, you'd probably be shocked. It is just covered with my husband’s appointment papers. He had to go to the specialist last Tuesday, and the parking at that clinic is just terrible now, they make you walk all the way from the back lot, and with his bad knee it takes us twenty minutes just to get to the elevator. 

But anyway, his papers are piled up there, right on top of all my church flyers. I was supposed to sort those out for the spring bazaar. Susan usually helps me with that, but she just moved to Ohio to be closer to her grandkids. They just had twins, you know, a boy and a girl. Oh, they are so cute in the pictures she sends. 

So the flyers are there, and my notes from the senior center, and just... all these half-finished lists I started. And I just sit down at that table, looking at all of it, and I simply don't know which thing to do first. I just sit there staring at the mess, and before I know it, the whole day is just gone.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states she cannot get anything in order, describing a messy table full of mixed papers and half-finished lists.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient's speech demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts, as she frequently interrupts her own narrative to discuss clinic parking and a friend's grandchildren.
symptom_reasoning.S031: The patient describes severe indecisiveness, stating she sits at the table not knowing which thing to do first until the whole day is gone.

turns.doctor_question: Have you always been this way with organizing and making decisions, or is this a new problem?
turns.patient_response:
Oh... no, it’s definitely not new. It’s funny you ask that, because I was just looking at some old keepsakes... well, I was actually supposed to be bringing down the winter coats from the hall closet, but I found a box with my old report cards instead. And even as a little girl, my teachers always wrote that I was bright but careless. I was always forgetting my books and my homework, and they'd have to give me constant reminders to just finish my seatwork before I could go outside. 

And oh, I just loved going outside. We had this huge oak tree behind the schoolhouse, and my friends and I used to collect the acorns. My brother Thomas would try to throw them at the squirrels, which was just terrible of him, but boys will be boys, I suppose. He’s living in Florida now, actually, playing golf every single day. I don't know how he stands the humidity down there. My hair just frizzes right up the second I step off the plane, and the bugs are simply enormous. I told him he ought to move back up north, but he says he can't stand the snow anymore... 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, organizing. Yes, I suppose it's always been this way for me.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient mentions needing constant reminders to finish her seatwork at school.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient confirms that she has always had problems with organizing.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by abandoning her task of getting winter coats because she found and started looking through a box of old report cards.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient states she was 'always forgetting my books and my homework'.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality, wandering from report cards to an oak tree, her brother, Florida, humidity, and bugs before losing her train of thought.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often lose track of things you need, like keys, paperwork, or appointments?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, goodness, yes. I am forever hunting for things I just had right in my hand a second ago. My car keys, my reading glasses... I actually bought three pairs of those little readers from the pharmacy just last week because I keep setting them down. They had a sale, buy two get one free, and the cashier was such a lovely young girl. She reminded me of my niece, Sarah, who just started college. She's studying marine biology, which I think is just fascinating. She wants to work with dolphins! We went to that big aquarium down in Atlanta years ago when she was little, and she just fell in love with them. 

But what was I... oh, losing things. Yes, appointment cards, too. And my recipes! Just the other day I was looking everywhere for my recipe for the church supper. I make this wonderful green bean casserole, the one with the crispy onions on top? Everyone just loves it, Pastor Miller always goes back for seconds. His wife, Brenda, she usually makes a pecan pie, but her oven has been acting up lately. Getting a repairman out these days is just impossible, they give you a window between 8 AM and 5 PM, so you just have to sit there all day. I can't stand waiting around like that, it just feels like such a waste of a day. 

And paperwork, yes, it's terrible. Last week I was tearing the house apart looking for the folder I needed to take to the doctor’s office. My husband's cardiologist, Dr. Evans. He has the loveliest waiting room, they have this big saltwater fish tank. I could watch those little yellow fish for hours, they just dart back and forth so quickly. I always wonder who cleans it, because keeping a fish tank clean is an awful lot of work. We had goldfish when the kids were small and the tank was always getting cloudy... but yes, I'm always losing track of those sorts of things.

symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly confirms frequently losing items like car keys, reading glasses, appointment cards, recipes, and paperwork.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts, frequently losing her train of thought to talk about her niece, a church supper, and a fish tank.
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, providing a long, rambling response to a straightforward question.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality and loose associations, drifting far from the original topic into unrelated stories before catching herself.

turns.doctor_question: Do these attention and organization problems happen in more than one setting, such as both at home and at work or with errands?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, yes, it’s everywhere. It’s not just at home with the kitchen table. When I go to the grocery store, it’s just as bad. I’ll walk in with a list—well, if I remember to bring the list, which I usually don't. I'll leave it right on the counter next to the toaster. We have one of those nice four-slice toasters now, my daughter bought it for us at Christmas because she said the old one was a fire hazard. It was perfectly fine, just a little temperamental if you pushed the lever too hard. But the new one is stainless steel and it shows every single fingerprint. I feel like I'm constantly wiping it down with a damp cloth. 

But at the store, I’ll go in for milk and eggs, and then I’ll see the bakery section. They have these wonderful blueberry muffins, the big ones with the sugar crystals on top? And I'll think, oh, I should get some of those for when the ladies from the garden club come over. We're planning the spring planting schedule, and we really need to figure out what to do about the deer eating all the hostas. They are just a menace this year. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, put up this tall wire fence, but I think it looks just dreadful, like a prison yard. I'd rather plant marigolds, I read somewhere that deer don't like the smell of them. 

So I'll be looking at the muffins, and then I'll wander over to the floral department, and before I know it, I've been in there for an hour, my cart is full of things I didn't need, and I completely forgot the milk. And errands, oh my. Going to the post office is an ordeal. I went last week to mail a package to my grandson for his birthday—he turned twelve, can you believe it? They grow up so fast. He's playing baseball now, he's the pitcher. But I got to the counter and realized I'd left the package in the trunk of the car. So I had to go all the way back out, and by the time I got back in, the line was out the door. So yes, it really does happen no matter where I am or what I'm trying to do.

symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by the bakery and floral departments while grocery shopping, causing her to forget her original purpose.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient frequently forgets things during daily errands, such as forgetting her grocery list, forgetting to buy milk, and leaving a package in the car at the post office.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality, wandering far off-topic to discuss her new toaster, garden club, deer, and her grandson's baseball before returning to the point.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel restless or fidgety, like you have trouble sitting still?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, goodness, yes. I try so hard to just sit still, especially when I'm supposed to be sitting politely, like at the garden club committee meetings. But I'll catch myself rubbing my hands together constantly, or tapping my foot under the table... or I'll have a pen and I'm just click-click-clicking it without even realizing. I shift around in my chair so much that the other ladies actually stop and look over at me. 

It's terribly embarrassing when Mary catches me doing it. Mary is the president of the club this year, and she runs a very tight ship. She used to be a high school principal, you know, over at Westside? My daughter went there, actually. She played the flute in the marching band, and those uniforms they had to wear were just made of the thickest, scratchiest wool. I don't know who on earth thought wool was a good idea for August in the marching band. We spent half the summer trying to get the band boosters to raise money for new ones, we did bake sales and car washes... I must have baked fifty dozen chocolate chip cookies that year. I always use my grandmother's recipe, the secret is a little dash of cinnamon and browning the butter first. It makes the whole house smell just heavenly. My husband would always try to sneak a few right off the cooling rack before the chocolate had even set... 

Wait, what was the question? Oh! Sitting still. Yes, I just can't seem to stop fidgeting and shifting around, even when everyone is looking right at me.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly describes rubbing her hands, tapping her foot, clicking a pen, and shifting around in her chair.

turns.doctor_question: Did these attention and organizing problems start before you were 12 years old?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, my, yes. Even when I was a little girl, my mother used to say my head was in the clouds. I remember my teachers—Mrs. Gable, she was my third-grade teacher, she had the most beautiful handwriting. It was that perfect Palmer method cursive, you know? She used to make us do those loops on lined paper for what felt like hours. I tried so hard to make my letters look like hers, but my pencil would always slip or I'd get distracted by the birds outside the window. We had a big oak tree right outside the classroom, and the squirrels would chase each other round and round the trunk. They were so busy! 

But Mrs. Gable, she used to write on my report cards that I was a bright girl, but just so careless. I was always forgetting my reading books or leaving my homework on the kitchen table. My mother would get so exasperated with me. She had this lovely oak dining table, the kind with the claw feet? It belonged to her grandmother, and she polished it every single Sunday with lemon oil. The whole house would smell like lemons and Sunday roast. She made the best pot roast, with those little pearl onions and carrots that were so tender they just melted in your mouth. I've tried to make it like hers, but I can never get the gravy quite right. Mine always turns out a little lumpy. My husband says he doesn't mind, bless his heart, but I know it's not the same.

What was I... oh, yes, being a little girl. Yes, I was always forgetting things, and Mrs. Gable would have to remind me over and over to finish my seatwork before I was allowed to go out for recess. I just couldn't seem to keep my mind on the paper in front of me.
